item.title: Issa visits north to assess support for vulnerable communities
item.description: The U.S. Embassy in Beirut said the United States remains “committed to delivering lifesaving humanitarian assistance and supporting durable solutions for vulnerable communities across Lebanon,” after U.S. Ambassador Michel Issa made a recent visit to North Lebanon and Akkar.

item.title: 19 hurt as Israel strikes southern towns and Lebanon-Syria border
item.description: The Israeli military said it struck four crossings along the Syria-Lebanon border on Wednesday that were allegedly used by Hezbollah to smuggle weapons, after earlier launching fresh strikes in south Lebanon.

item.title: UK, US and Canada reaffirm support for Lebanese Army at High-Level Steering Committee
item.description: British Ambassador to Lebanon Hamish Cowell, U.S. Ambassador, Michel Issa, and Canadian Ambassador Gregory Galligan met Lebanese Army chief General Rodolphe Haykal during the High-Level Steering Committee (HLSC) meeting on Wednesday. “The Committee convened to review progress and challenges in securing Lebanon’s eastern and northern borders, and reaffirmed support for the LAF’s (Lebanese Army’s) efforts to reinforce state authority at this critical time,” the British embassy said.

item.title: Salam says Hezbollah disarmament 'historic moment' in 'very difficult' climate
item.description: Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said that Hezbollah's disarmament south of the Litani river is "a historic moment in a very difficult environment". Salam said, in an interview, on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos on Wednesday, that Lebanon is "slowly but surely" regaining the trust of the international community and is moving to the second phase of disarming Hezbollah - north of the Litani.

item.title: Salam confident Lebanon can improve banking draft law for IMF endorsement
item.description: The International Monetary Fund has asked the Lebanese government to amend a banking draft law that would allow depositors to recover their funds and said it can't endorse the draft "as presented". The law, a key demand from the international community to unblock economic aid to Lebanon, was approved last month by the Lebanese government. It stipulates that each of the state, the central bank, commercial banks and depositors will share the losses accrued as a result of the financial crisis.

item.title: Condemnation no longer sufficient, Berri says after violent Wednesday strikes
item.description: Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri called for "national unity" after a long day of violent Israeli strikes on south Lebanon and on crossings along the Syria-Lebanon border. "Statements of condemnation are no longer sufficient," Berri said, adding that only national unity can save Lebanon.

item.title: Trump says 'we have to do something' about Hezbollah
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that “something” must be done about Hezbollah in Lebanon.

item.title: Report: Army about to finalize national security strategy
item.description: The Lebanese Army is preparing the national security strategy that President Joseph Aoun had pledged to devise in his inaugural speech, a media report said.

item.title: Bassil agrees with KSA on state sovereignty, rejects country's partitioning
item.description: Free Patriotic Movement chief Jebran Bassil said Thursday he agrees with Saudi Arabia on many issues, including unity and the state's monopoly on arms. Bassil said the partition of Lebanon would not benefit the Christians in the country, amid divisions and a "clear" shifting of borders in the region.

item.title: Israel's destruction of Lebanon's environment raises international law questions
item.description: By Mireille Rebeiz, Dickinson College and Josiane Yazbeck, Université La Sagesse (THE CONVERSATION) More than a year after a ceasefire nominally ended active fighting, much of southern Lebanon bears the ecological scars of war. Avocado orchards are gone and beehives destroyed. So, too, are the livelihoods they supported. Meanwhile, fields and forests have disappeared under the intense fire caused by white phosphorus shelling. Shrapnel and unexploded bombs, however, remain.
